set.hook: Lefteris Lazarou's seafood room on the Mikrolimano quay, the top-scored Greek-cuisine kitchen of 2026.
set.why: Lefteris Lazarou, a ship's cook's son who first cooked at sea at fifteen, opened Varoulko in 1987 and in 2002 won the first MICHELIN Star ever given to Greek cooking. The Star was gone by the Athens 2024 selection, which lists the room without one. Greek critics did not follow: in May 2026 Athinorama's Greek Cuisine Awards again scored it 16/20, the highest Greek-cuisine mark in the country. The seaside room on the Mikrolimano boardwalk opened in 2013.
set.hours: Call ahead: the MICHELIN listing gives daily 13:00-24:00; Mes Prestiges (checked May 2026) gives Tue-Sun 13:00-24:00, closed Monday; other undated listings give daily 12:30-24:00 or 13:00-01:00

set.hook: A third-generation Mikrolimano fish house from 1932, built on raw shellfish and fish salt-grilled over coals.
set.why: Giorgos Dourabeis, from Ios, and Rallia, from Kythira, opened this fish house on the harbour in 1932; their grandsons Sergios, Kostas and Rallis run it now. A 2005 renovation stripped out the old taverna look, which is why the room reads formal rather than rustic. The FNL Guide kept it among its starred Athens tables in 2026, and in 2023 the Brazilian chef Alex Atala of D.O.M. in Sao Paulo chose it for an Athens meal and posted about it.

set.hook: Chef Giorgos Papaioannou's Mikrolimano waterfront room, where the day's catch is grilled and left alone.
set.why: Giorgos Papaioannou learned to cook fish from his father in an early-1990s back-street shop near the port, then moved the flagship onto the Mikrolimano waterfront in spring 2013. The name has since spread to Kefalari, Kavouri and a Mykonos outpost under the Okyalos group, and in May 2026 Athinorama's Greek Cuisine Awards scored the Mikrolimano room 14.5 out of 20.

set.hook: A 1944 fried-fish room by the Naval Academy with no menu, no bookings and the family's own retsina.
set.why: Margaro, a woman from Ano Mera on Mykonos, started frying fish on this corner in 1944. Her son Lazaros took over in 1974 and cut the list to what it still is: four or five fried catches, a Greek salad and retsina from the family's vines in Markopoulo. Her grandchildren work the pans now. Guides list shrimp, crayfish, red mullet, koutsomoura and lithrini, all pan-fried and never grilled, with tables spilling into the street in good weather.

set.hook: A Kastella hilltop fish taverna since 1957, looking down over the port and out to the Saronic.
set.why: Before it was a taverna it was a 1930s kafenio selling coffee and snacks to the Kastella neighbourhood. In 1957 Paraschos Manioudakis, a Cretan who had come to Piraeus for dock work, turned it into a taverna beside the chapel of Profitis Ilias. His grandson later renovated the room and kept the menu as it was. The terrace appears in the 1971 heist film The Burglars, and on a clear day the view runs from the Acropolis to Aegina.

set.hook: A canteen inside the Keratsini fish auction, frying and grilling the morning's catch beside the docks.
set.why: The Keratsini ichthyoskala has stood on the Iraklis harbour since 1965 and auctions fish every day of the year. Vasilis and Valbona, who came from Albania as newlyweds, took over its abandoned canteen in 2018 and rebuilt it from tarps and pallets; their daughter Alexandra works the tables. He crosses to the opposite dock around 3 a.m. to choose the fish, and octopus charred over coals is what the regulars order.

set.hook: A husband-and-wife ouzeri on Keratsini's little harbour, cooking what the local caiques landed.
set.why: Chrysa and Giorgos have kept this ouzeri on Keratsini's little harbour for more than thirty years, under the chimney of the closed DEH power station and in sight of the COSCO container cranes. The supply line is short: the harbour's fishermen eat half of what they land and sell Giorgos the rest, so the red mullet and anchovies are usually that morning's. Ask what is best today and they will tell you plainly.

set.hook: A former ship captain's small seafood ouzeri in Hatzikyriakio, its walls hung with his maritime collection.
set.why: Andreas Kontsos captained ships out of Kimolos before he cooked, and he kept what the sea left him: anchors, ropes, ocean-liner memorabilia. After running the 1990s Piraeus spot Karpouzi, he opened this small room in a former nautical warehouse and named it after the liners that carried Greek emigrants to Australia. On good nights there is ladenia, the Kimolos tomato-and-onion flatbread, next to the charcoal sardines.

set.hook: A producer-led meze room in a 1920 Freattyda neoclassical, with a roof terrace in summer.
set.why: The house is a 1920 neoclassical built by an architect who arrived by boat from Constantinople and settled in Freattyda. set.hook: An Ikarian sailors' kafenio near the port gates: tsipouro, tavli and mezedes that arrive unasked.
set.why: For about seventy years this kafenio has poured for the Ikarian community of Piraeus, its walls covered with photographs and murals of the island. Sailors and shipyard hands come for tsipouro with cheese and olives brought from Ikaria. When the 1956 building on Akti Poseidonos that housed it was taken back for redevelopment, the regulars moved the whole kafenio a few streets inland; LiFO reported the move in August 2023. Nikos, 'the Ikarian', keeps the counter.

set.hook: A 1920 grocery and wine shop near the port, still pouring the family's own retsina beside simple fry-ups.
set.why: Aristeidis Papakonstantinou came down from Gardiki, near Trikala, and opened this grocery and wine shop in 1920; the same family has run it since. Holes in the metal shutter were left by German bullets during the Occupation and kept on purpose. The retsina is the family's own, and the plates are what a corner grocer would cook: fried liver, meatballs, potatoes under eggs. On some nights groups arrive with instruments and the room sings.
set.reservation: Walk in most days; book on live-music nights

set.hook: A 1958 koutouki in Palaia Kokkinia, its covered courtyard built around an old whitewashed fig tree.
set.why: The koutouki has cooked since 1958 in a lane above Thivon Street in Palaia Kokkinia, the quarter built by refugees after 1922. Its covered courtyard grows around a tall fig tree with a whitewashed trunk, among old tiles and small objects gathered over decades. The business registry names Eirini Vergopoulou as holder; the sign still carries the name of the original Antonis. Wine comes from the barrel by the karafa.

set.hook: A Nikaia meze house in a 1938 building, with Smyrna soutzoukakia and rebetiko trios at weekends
set.why: The name comes from an old island word for far away, and the Smyrna Association of Nikaia and Piraeus used the same word to title one of its own music-and-dance shows. The kitchen leans on the dishes the 1922 refugees carried west, starting with hand-rolled cumin soutzoukakia and pastourma pie, then goes off to the Tzoumerka for pork tigania and to Crete for snail stifado. On Saturdays a rebetiko trio plays the Smyrna repertoire.

set.hook: Drapetsona's oldest taverna, a 1930s dairy turned grill, known for Dora's ouzo-doused meatballs
set.why: It began around 1930 as a dairy shop opposite the church of Agios Panteleimon. Grigoris Katsogiannis started grilling salt cod and chops on charcoal, and by stages it became a grocery-taverna. Since 2005 Dora Stavridou has cooked here from family recipes: a handful of pot dishes that change daily, such as papoutsakia, moussaka and imam, plus fries she cuts by hand. A 1930 British Prestcold refrigerator with mirrored doors still stands in the room and still works.

set.hook: A daytime corner grill in the old flea-market lanes with a cult following for its beef-meatball wrap
set.why: Grigoris Tsakiris and his son Giorgos opened in 2019 among the junk dealers behind the fish market, wanting souvlaki the way it used to be made. The menu is short: a wrap of two small beef patties, mixed daily and grilled when you order, or a plate of six, with tomato, onion, parsley, red sauce and a hot pepper. The pita is their own recipe, made by hand without preservatives. There are no fries, no tzatziki and no other sauces.

set.hook: An Armenian refugee family's charcoal kebab on Plateia Neraidas, salt and pepper only, since 1972
set.why: Sarkis 'Serkos' Hanikyan reached Kokkinia among the Armenians who survived Smyrna. He sold nuts from a cart near the old Esperos cinema before learning to grind and grill kebab, and in 1972 he opened his first shop. The recipe has not changed since: beef and lamb mince, salt, pepper and charcoal, no strong spice. His children run the grill now, and the tables spill onto the square in the old refugee grid behind Thivon.
set.price_range: Kebab ~2 euros a piece; plate with two pitas, tomato, onion and tzatziki from ~9 euros (efood listing)

set.hook: A near-fifty-year-old gyro counter by Karaiskakis, its walls packed with Olympiacos memorabilia
set.why: The shop is a few minutes' walk from Olympiacos's Karaiskakis ground, and its walls are covered with the club's scarves, photographs and pennants. Spiros and Eleni have run it for about thirty of its nearly fifty years. They turn the gyro by hand and grill the patties and skewers in front of you, and they make the slightly hot red sauce that regulars come back for. The gyro can sell out early in the evening.

set.hook: Piraeus's oldest galaktopoleio, in the family since 1909, cutting galaktoboureko by the slab
set.why: The business started in 1909 as a dairy shop that also ran a taverna. The grandfather delivered milk by donkey around Profitis Ilias, and the family still keeps his tin milk can. Over time the taverna gave way to pastry, and galaktoboureko became the main trade: sheep's-butter custard under crisp phyllo, sold by the piece from big trays or in round pans, with a kataifi version too. Cookout/SKAI reported orders coming from as far as Sweden.
set.caveat: A sweets counter to take away from, with no savoury breakfast. A second branch operates in Pigada.

set.hook: A Pontic piroski workshop by the ferry gates, frying a Trebizond family recipe from before dawn
set.why: Parthenopi Amanatidou carried her piroski recipe from Trebizond to Constantinople, then to Greece in the 1922 expulsion. Her family says nostalgia for the lost city pushed her to open the first Pontic piroski workshop in Piraeus in 1976. In the 1990s her son Spyros, a sea captain often away for months, and his wife Vasiliki trained beside her to carry it on. The shop has since moved to Notara 50 and taken the name Euxeinon, the ancient name for the Black Sea.

set.hook: A round-the-clock phyllo workshop in Nikaia since 1974, still the port's reference bougatsa
set.why: Leonidas Pavlidis learned to stretch phyllo from a Pomak baker in Sapes, in Rhodope, and opened here in 1974, when Petrou Ralli was still unpaved. Through the 1970s to the 1990s, night-owl musicians came at three in the morning for sweet bougatsa instead of tripe soup. His daughter Sophia Dridaki-Pavlidi runs it now, with her son Giorgos learning the trade. To Vima wrote about it in March 2026, and it still bakes before dawn.
set.hours: Call ahead: LiFO and To Vima (Mar 2026) say open 24 hours; a Psaxno listing shows Wednesday closed

set.hook: A truckers' canteen at port Gate E2, grilling the pork skewers chef Vasilis Kallidis calls the city's best
set.why: The canteen stands among the trucks at Gate E2, opposite the Crete ferries, beside the derelict conveyor that once loaded fertiliser from the Lipasmata works onto ships. The owner, Fortetsanakis, is known as Plastiras and says he is a baptismal godson of General Nikolaos Plastiras, so the general's portraits cover the walls. Chef Vasilis Kallidis has named its pork kalamaki as his favourite street food and put it among the five best souvlaki in Athens.
set.hours: Call ahead: ask4food says from early morning, Mon-Fri; old record says it also runs late after nights out. Not reconciled
